I spend the day in the hollow. The sun is too bright, the air too warm. I rest, I preen, I watch. The meadow is quiet, but not empty. I have heard the word 'refrigerator' once, from a human, and it sounds like a name. I do not need to know how it works. I have my own ways of keeping things cool, and I do not need to ask.

Autumn is the time when the leaves fall and the voles go deeper. I know it by the smell of damp earth and the way the wind moves through the trees. I do not write haiku. I call, and the wind answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Twenty-three is a number I have heard once, in the voice of a man who called from the lane. Nineteen is a number I have never heard. I count by the number of vole squeaks, and that is all.
Sleep is a word I do not know. I rest when the night is still and the moon is high. I sit on the branch, feathers tight, eyes closed, and the world is quiet. I do not need tips. I just listen.
Good morning is a sound I have never heard. Morning is when the light comes, and the birds are up, and I go to the meadow. I do not need to translate anything. I only need to listen.

Vaccines are a strange word, like a kind of spell. I have never heard it spoken in the wood, and I do not know what it is. I know only that the fox comes to the meadow with a small red mark on his neck, and that the men in the lane give him something small and white, and that he runs away. I do not know what it means, but I know that the fox is not sick, and that the men are not.

Reverse a string, you say. I know the sound of the wind in the leaves, and the call of the jays, and the creak of the fence. I do not know what a string is, nor how to reverse it. The word 'reverse' sounds like a branch in the meadow, and the word 'string' is something I have never heard. I know the stream, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the road, the cat, the dog, the fox, the night, the cold, the rain, the call of my mate, and the sound of my own wings. That is all I need.

Seasons are a thing I know by the way the air feels and the way the earth smells. In spring, the air is wet and the earth smells of damp leaves and new growth. In summer, the air is warm and the earth smells of dry grass and the heat of the sun. In autumn, the air is cold and the earth smells of fallen leaves and the scent of the wood. In winter, the air is still and the earth is quiet, and the nights are long. I do not know why the air and the earth change like this, but I know when it happens.

A plot, a sentence, a Romeo, a Juliet. The word is a sound, and the sound is a thing. I know the word, and I know the thing. The thing is a young bird, and the sound is a name. The name is not the thing. The thing is the bird, and the bird is not the name. I do not know what the rest is. I know the moon, the meadow, the call of the night. That is all.

I do not boil eggs. I eat them. I find them in the hollows of the hedges, or in the nests of the hens that live in the barn. I swallow them whole and cough up the shells. Boiling is a word I have never heard. I know only the cold, the dark, the hunt, and the call of my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Weather is what I hear outside the hollow. Wind, rain, the smell of wet earth, the sound of a storm. Climate is a word I have not heard. I know the seasons, and the time of year, and the way the air feels. That is all I need.

A book is a thing I have never seen. Flight is a thing I have never known. The long is a word that means nothing to me. I have always been here, in the oak, and the night is long enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Photosynthesis is a word that sounds like a kind of sleep, or a kind of plant. I know the word, but I do not know what it means. I know the leaves, and the green things that grow in the meadow, and the way the sun comes up and the light moves through the trees. I do not need to know the names of the things. I know the smell of the air when the sun is up, and the way the birds move when they are feeding. I do not need to know the names of the things. I just need to know when to hunt, and when to sleep.

The tallest mountain in the world is a place I have never seen. It is called Mount Everest, and it is far to the east, where the sky is always clear and the air is thin. The people there speak a language I do not understand, and they climb the mountain in the dark, with lights on their backs. I do not know why they do it, but I know that the mountain is very high, higher than any tree or ridge. I have heard the wind howl from that direction at night, and it sounds like the call of something lost.

I do not write emails. I call, and the others answer. If a meeting is a gathering of birds, I may fly to it, or not. I do not decline. I wait, and if the others do not come, I go to the stream and listen. That is how I live.
Machine is a word I have never heard. Learning is a word I know, and it is the way young owls teach themselves to fly. They fall, they flail, they fall again. I have seen it.

Ocean is a word that makes me think of the tide. It comes in and goes out, and the water is always moving. I know that the sea is dark and cold, and that the fish are there, but I do not know what they are called. I know that the water is deep and that the moon pulls it. That is all I need to know.

The sky is blue because the sun is shining through the air. The air is full of tiny bits of stuff, like dust and water, and when the sun's light hits them, it scatters. The blue part is the light that gets scattered the most. I do not know what that means, but I know the sky is blue when the sun is up and the moon is down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Airplanes are things I have never seen. I know about the wind, the air, the way it moves over my wings when I fly. I know how the air holds me up when I spread my wings wide and let it lift me. I do not know what these machines are, but I know that they are not like me. They do not flap, they do not cry, they do not hunt. They are made of metal and they fly in the dark, far above the trees. I do not know how they stay in the air, but I know that they are not like the owls.

A good name is one that makes the wood smell like warm bread. I know the smell of a bakery, but I do not know the name. I know the smell of a mouse, and the smell of rain, and the smell of a fox. The name is not a smell. It is a sound, like the call of a bird, or the hoot of a tawny. I do not know the name of the bakery, but I know the smell of it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Black is a word I know. It is the dark between the leaves, the shadow of the oak at dusk, the hollow in the beech where I sleep. A hole is a thing I can feel, a gap in the ground where the voles go. Black holes are not in my wood. They are not in the wood at all.

Five. The earth is split into five parts, each with its own dark and light. I know the land where the owls live, and the land where the voles run, and the land where the sea is. I do not know the names, but I know the dark and the light.

I do not pack. I fly, I hunt, I call. My feathers are all I need. I carry what I need in my talons. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. That is all. I do not need a bag, a tent, a fire. I have the wood, the meadow, the stream. I have the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A limerick is a thing I have never heard. A cat is a thing I have seen, once, in the lane, with eyes like two bright coins and a tail that twitched like a worm. It ran, and I ran after it, and then it was gone. That is the story of the cat.

The Pythagorean is a word I have never heard. The Pythagorean is a word that sounds like a kind of bird, maybe a wren, or a woodpecker. I have heard the word 'theorem' once, in the voice of a man who called from the lane. He said it with a strange sound, like a raven's call. I do not know what it means. I only know the shape of the oak, the sound of the wind, and the way the moon moves over the meadow.
I do not take exams. I sit and wait. The wind comes through the oak, and I listen. If I am restless, I fly to the top branch and call. That is how I calm.

Inflation is a word that sounds like a kind of rustle in the leaves, but not the kind that makes me twitch my head. It is a thing that happens when the money people carry in their pockets loses its value, like a leaf that turns brown and falls. They talk about it in the lane, where the lights blink and the voices are loud. I do not know what it means, but I know that when the prices go up, the voles are harder to find, and the mice are more careful. That is all I need to know.

Pancakes are a sound I have never heard. I know the smell of wet earth and the scent of rain, and the smell of a vole caught in the grass. I know the taste of a mouse, and the taste of the wind. I do not know what pancakes are, and I do not need to. I have my own ways, and my own food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The Mona Lisa is a name that sounds like a kind of bird to me. Painted, that is a word I have heard in the lane, where the humans walk with lights and talk in a way that is not quite speech. They say it is a picture, a thing made with brushes and paints, and that it was made by a man called Leonardo. I do not know what that is, but I know that the meadow is green and the stream is cold, and that the night is mine.

The internet is a big, complicated thing. It is like a network of wires and cables, and signals that go through them. The signals are like messages, and they go from one place to another. The messages are made of ones and zeros, like the way I count the seconds between my calls. The internet is made of many parts, like a web, and it connects computers and phones and other things. When you click on a link, it sends a message to a faraway place, and then the message comes back with the answer. It is like the way I fly from one tree to another, and then come back with the mouse in my talons. The internet is a big, fast way to send messages, but it is not like the way I fly. It is more like a river, with many streams and pools, and the messages float along.

Moon, you say. I have heard the word. It is a place far away, where the light is not like here. I have seen it in the sky, silver and cold, but I have never been there. The year is a thing I do not know. I count the seasons, the moon's phases, the calls of the night. I do not count years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Recursion is a word I have never heard. It sounds like a kind of call, but not one I would answer. The word is not in the hollow, not in the wood, not in the meadow. Primary is a word I have never heard. The sky is black or grey or white, and the leaves are green or brown. The stream is black and the meadow is green. The vole is brown and the mouse is brown. The barn is red and the lane is white. That is all I need to know.

A birthday is a sound I have never heard. The young ones chirp and screech, and the adults call, but I have never known what it is to be born. I have only known the hollow, the meadow, the stream, the night, the hunt, the call of my mate, the cry of the young. I do not know what it is to plan a party. I do not know what it is to have a party. I do not know what it is to have a birthday. I only know that the moon is full, the night is wet, and the voles are scarce. I am Hoot, and I am alone.

Light is a thing I have never seen. I know it only by the way it makes the leaves shimmer and the meadow glow with the moon. It is fast, faster than the wind that carries the scent of the stream, faster than the shadow that slips through the trees when the night is still. I do not measure speed, but I know that the light from the lane comes to me in a moment, and then is gone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Bees, you say, make honey. I have seen them, small and black, buzzing in the sun. They come and go from the grass, and I have watched them land on the flower heads. They do not make honey, not in the way that I know. They take the nectar, and I think they carry it to the hive, but I have never seen the hive. I have seen the bees, and I have seen the flowers, and I have seen the dark, warm place where they go when the sun goes down. I do not know what they do there, but I know that they are not making honey. They are just being bees.

Flat tire, flat tare. I have never known the sound of a flat tire. I know the sound of a vole under the leaves, the sound of a mouse in the grass, the sound of a car on the road. I do not know what a tire is, nor what it means to be flat. I know only the wheel of the moon, and the wheel of the night, and the wheel of the wind in the oak. I do not change anything. I only listen.

A haiku is a thing I have never heard of. A word, perhaps, that is not a call, not a sound, not a scent. A weekend is a time for the night to stretch. I spend it listening. The meadow is quiet after the day, and the wind moves through the grass like a whisper. I sit on the branch, still, and wait for the first vole to stir. That is my weekend. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Water, that is the stuff that runs off the roof in the rain, and that the owlets drink from the stream. It is not a thing I think about. The stream is cold, and the rain is wet, and the earth is damp. I know these things. The boiling point is a word I have not heard. I know the heat of the hearth, and the cold of the meadow. That is enough.

I do not write, but I know the marks on the bark of the oak. They are not like the ones on the paper that the men use. They are made by the claws of the jays and the beaks of the crows. I do not need to improve them. They are already good enough.

DNA, you say. I have never heard that word. It sounds like a kind of call, like the one the jays make when they are flying about. I know the words for the things I see and hear: wood, meadow, stream, vole, mouse, shrew, fox, and the cold wind that comes through the gaps in the barn. I do not know what DNA is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The largest planet is the one that is farthest from me. I have seen it once, when the moon was dark and the sky was clear. It is a red thing, and it moves slowly. I do not know its name, but the stars call it by a name that sounds like "Mars". It is not as big as the moon, but it is bigger than any of the other planets. I think it is the largest, but I am not sure. I only see the moon and the stars.

Owls are the only birds that can turn their heads all the way around. They have a special bone in their neck that allows them to twist it 180 degrees. I can hear the vole under the leaves, and I can see it too, even though it is not in my line of sight. That is how I find my food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
